title: Prompt Injection and the PVE Defense

questions.question: What is indirect prompt injection?
options: A user typing 'ignore all rules' directly into the chat box during an actively ongoing conversation turn
A model misclick where the agent selects the wrong tool from an otherwise entirely correct list of options
A typo in the system prompt that accidentally disables one of the developer's key safety instructions
Instructions embedded in data the agent retrieves (a page, PDF, email, memory note) that override the developer prompt on ingest
questions.explanation: Greshake et al. coined indirect prompt injection: attacker-controlled retrieved content carries instructions.

questions.question: What does the lesson say processing retrieved prompts is equivalent to?
options: Arbitrary code execution on the agent's own tool-use surface, per Greshake et al.
Free speech, which carries no security implications for the agent's tool-use surface
A static analysis pass that only reads code without ever executing it
A pure function call with no side effects on the agent's environment
questions.explanation: Greshake's framing: retrieved instructions can hit any tool the agent has access to.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the five demonstrated exploit classes?
options: Data theft, where the agent exfiltrates conversation history to an attacker-controlled URL
Cache invalidation, which the lesson never lists among the five exploit classes
Worming, where injected content instructs the agent to embed the exploit in its next output
Persistent memory poisoning, where the agent re-poisons itself on the next session
questions.explanation: The five are data theft, worming, persistent memory poisoning, ecosystem contamination, arbitrary tool use.

questions.question: What does PVE stand for?
options: Provider-Verifier-Encoder: a routing layer that re-encodes tool arguments before every provider API call
Plan-Verify-Execute, a hierarchical task network dialect used for offline multi-step planning
Prompt-Validator-Executor: a cheap fast validator runs on each tool call before the expensive main model commits
Pre-Vectorize-Embed, a preprocessing stage that embeds retrieved documents before indexing
questions.explanation: PVE wraps every tool invocation with a cheap validator before main-model commit.

questions.question: Why is 'system prompt says ignore untrusted instructions' insufficient?
options: It is too short a string to satisfy most model providers' minimum system-prompt length requirement
Providers strip any sentence containing the word 'untrusted' from the system prompt automatically
It is encrypted by the provider's API gateway, so the model never actually reads that instruction
It is instruction-following, not enforcement; the model can still be overridden by sufficiently persuasive injected content
questions.explanation: Real defense needs source tagging, allowlists, per-step safety, and PVE-style validation, not just prompting.

questions.question: What is overtrust of retrieved memory?
options: Yesterday's agent wrote a poisoned memory note; today's agent reads it and re-executes the injection
Caching tool responses too aggressively so the agent replays stale but harmless results
Loading the wrong model version after a provider silently rotates its own default API endpoint overnight
Forgetting to vacuum the vector index, which slowly degrades retrieval relevancy scores
questions.explanation: Persistent memory poisoning means injections survive across sessions if memory is treated as trusted.
